title: Investing Basics
description: Make your money hunt while you sleep.
wolfLine: Time in the market beats timing the market.

investing.definition: Putting money into something you expect to grow in value over time.
investing.example: Buying a small piece of a company and holding it for years.

return.definition: How much your investment grew (or shrank), often shown as a percentage.
return.example: Invest $1,000, it becomes $1,080: an $80 return, or 8%.

compound-growth.definition: When your returns start earning returns of their own, so growth speeds up over time.
compound-growth.example: $1,000 grows 10% to $1,100. Next year's 10% is on $1,100, not $1,000.

rule-of-72.definition: A shortcut: divide 72 by your yearly return to see roughly how many years it takes to double your money.
rule-of-72.example: At 8% a year: 72 ÷ 8 = about 9 years to double.

stock.definition: A tiny piece of ownership in a company. Also called a share.
stock.example: Own one share of a coffee chain and you own a sliver of every café.

bond.definition: A loan you give to a company or government. They pay you interest, then return your money at the end.
bond.example: Lend $1,000 to the government for 5 years and get interest every year.

risk.definition: The chance that an investment drops in value, or swings up and down a lot.
risk.example: A single company's stock can fall 50% in a bad year. That's high risk.

dividend.definition: A share of a company's profit, paid out to the people who own its stock.
dividend.example: You own 10 shares and the company pays $1 per share: you get $10.

portfolio.definition: All of your investments, taken together.
portfolio.example: A few stocks, one bond and an index fund make up your portfolio.

fund.definition: A pot of money from lots of people, invested in many things at once. You buy a slice of the pot.
fund.example: One purchase gets you a little of hundreds of companies.

index.definition: A list that tracks a group of investments, like a country's biggest companies.
index.example: A list of the 500 largest companies in one country.

index-fund.definition: A fund that simply buys everything on an index, instead of trying to pick winners. Usually cheap.
index-fund.example: One index fund can own all 500 companies on a list.

expense-ratio.definition: The yearly fee a fund charges, as a percentage of what you've invested.
expense-ratio.example: A 0.1% expense ratio on $10,000 costs $10 a year.

diversification.definition: Spreading your money across lots of different investments, so one bad one can't sink you.
diversification.example: Owning hundreds of companies in many countries instead of just one.

concentration-risk.definition: The danger of having too much money in one place. If that one thing fails, you lose big.
concentration-risk.example: All your savings in the company you work for.

lessons.title: Compound Growth
lessons.summary: Returns that earn their own returns.

steps.context: [[Investing]] means putting money into something you expect to grow in value. The growth you get is your [[return]].
steps.prompt: You invest $1,000 and a year later it's worth $1,080. What's the extra $80?
steps.explain: Your money grew by $80. That's your return, or 8%.

steps.context: Returns are usually a percentage. A 10% return on $1,000 is $1,000 × 0.10 = $100, so you'd have $1,100.
steps.prompt: You invest $2,000 and earn a 10% return in a year. What's it worth now?

steps.context: With [[compound growth]], next year's return is earned on your original money **plus** last year's return. Growth earns more growth.
steps.prompt: Your $1,000 grew to $1,100. Next year, you'll earn a return on…
steps.explain: Last year's return is now working for you too.

steps.prompt: That $1,100 earns another 10% in year two. What's it worth now?
steps.explain: $1,100 × 1.10 = $1,210. The extra $10 is growth on last year's growth.

steps.context: Here's a shortcut, the [[Rule of 72]]. Divide 72 by your yearly return to see roughly how many years your money takes to double. At 8%: 72 ÷ 8 = 9 years.
steps.prompt: Roughly how many years does it take to double your money at 6% a year?
Starting to invest 10 years earlier can matter more than investing a bigger amount later.
steps.explain: Early money gets more years of compound growth. Time beats size.

steps.context: A [[stock]] (also called a share) is a tiny piece of ownership in a company. If the company does well, your piece can become worth more.
steps.prompt: You buy a stock in a coffee chain. What do you now own?
choices: A tiny piece of the company
steps.explain: You're a part-owner. A very small one.

steps.context: A [[bond]] is a loan **you** give to a company or government. They pay you interest, then hand your money back at the end.
steps.prompt: You buy a government bond. What are you doing?
steps.explain: You're the lender this time. They pay you interest.

steps.context: [[Risk]] is the chance your investment drops or swings around a lot. Stocks swing more than bonds, so they're riskier, but over long periods they've usually grown more.
steps.prompt: Which is usually riskier?
steps.explain: Bigger swings, bigger long-run growth. That's the trade.

steps.context: Some companies share part of their profit with the people who own their stock. That payment is a [[dividend]].
steps.prompt: You own a stock and the company pays you a slice of its profit. What's that called?
steps.explain: Profit shared with owners. That's you.

steps.context: Everything you've invested in, taken together, is your [[portfolio]].
steps.prompt: You own a few stocks and one bond. What's that collection called?
steps.explain: All your investments, in one word.

steps.prompt: Recap: match each word to what it means.
pairs: A loan that pays you interest

steps.prompt: You'll need your money in one year for a house deposit. What fits better?
choices: Mostly safe, steady places like a savings account
steps.explain: Stocks can drop right before you need the cash. Short timeline, low risk.

lessons.title: Index Funds
lessons.summary: Buy the whole haystack instead of hunting for the needle.

steps.context: A [[fund]] pools money from lots of people and invests it in many things at once. You buy a slice of the pot.
steps.prompt: Why do people buy funds?
choices: To own lots of investments with one purchase
To make sure they never lose money
steps.explain: One purchase, many investments.

steps.context: An [[index]] is a list that tracks a group of companies, like a country's 500 biggest. An [[index fund]] simply buys everything on that list.
steps.prompt: What does an index fund do?
choices: Buys every company on a list
steps.explain: No guessing which company wins. You own them all.

steps.context: Every fund charges a yearly fee called the [[expense ratio]], a percentage of what you've invested. Index funds are usually cheap.
steps.prompt: Two funds own the same things. One's expense ratio is 1%, the other's is 0.1%. Which leaves you more money?
steps.explain: Lower fee, more left for you.

steps.prompt: You have $50,000 in a fund with a 1% expense ratio. What's the fee each year?
steps.explain: $50,000 × 0.01 = $500, every single year.

steps.prompt: Same $50,000 in a fund with a 0.1% expense ratio. What's the fee each year?

steps.context: Some funds pay experts to pick stocks and try to beat an index. Over long periods, most of them end up behind once their higher fees are counted.
steps.prompt: Paying an expert to pick stocks usually beats an index fund over the long run.
steps.explain: Most fall behind after fees. That's why index funds are so popular.

lessons.title: Diversification
lessons.summary: Don't let one bad bet sink the pack.

steps.context: [[Diversification]] means spreading your money across lots of different investments, so one bad one can't sink you.
steps.prompt: Which portfolio is more diversified?
choices: All your money in one company
An index fund holding hundreds of companies
Three companies in the same industry
steps.explain: Hundreds of companies means no single one can wipe you out.

steps.context: Having too much money in one place is called [[concentration risk]]. If that one thing fails, you lose big.
steps.prompt: Which of these has the most concentration risk?
choices: A mix of stocks and bonds
All your savings in the company you work for
steps.explain: If the company struggles, you could lose your job and your savings at once.

steps.prompt: A diversified portfolio can never lose money.
steps.explain: When everything falls, it falls too. Just less painfully than one bad bet.

steps.context: You can diversify in lots of ways: across companies, industries, countries, and types of investment.
steps.prompt: Match each way to diversify with an example.
Why mix stocks and bonds in one portfolio?
choices: They often move differently, which smooths out the ride
steps.explain: When one dips, the other often holds steady.

steps.prompt: Spreading your money across many investments is called ___.
steps.explain: Spread out so no single hit takes you down.

Move it all into one stock that's holding up
steps.explain: Drops are the price of admission. Panic is the expensive part.
